title: Dolls and Dolls, Guys!
summary: Josh and Chuck's Christmas Day episode on dolls in general. They discuss the loose definition of a doll, developmental benefits (empathy, caregiving, perspective taking), gender marketing of toys from the 1940s and pink/blue color coding, and the etymology of "doll" as a nickname for Dorothy. Historical coverage includes Egyptian paddle dolls, Roman and Greek dolls, the oldest rag doll in North America (Bangwell Putt), Victorian porcelain dolls and death kits, and dollhouses. The hosts cover Black dolls, including the topsy turvy doll, Jim Crow-era racist dolls, the Clark doll tests cited in Brown v. Board of Education, Sarah Lee and Baby Nancy. Other topics are paper dolls, Raggedy Ann, Betsy Wetsy, Magic Potty Baby, Chatty Kathy and Edison's talking doll, Polly Pocket, American Girl dolls, realistic reborn baby dolls and their use with dementia patients, Hasbro's Mr. Mucho/Buddy L-style boys' doll G.I. Joe-era macho doll, pediophobia (fear of dolls), and creepy dolls like Little Miss No Name and Creepy Chloe.
topics: oldest rag doll in North America

segments.title: Christmas greeting and episode setup
segments.summary: The hosts greet listeners on Christmas and introduce the annual toy episode about dolls in general, beyond Cabbage Patch Kids.

segments.title: Defining dolls and developmental benefits
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how hard it is to define a doll, noting that a doll is generally a human-like figure, excluding puppets, action figures, and stuffed animals. They describe how dolls help children develop empathy, emotional recognition, caregiving skills, and perspective taking.

segments.title: Gender marketing of toys and dolls
segments.summary: Dolls became associated with girls partly because of 1940s marketing that split toys by gender. The hosts note pink became a girls' color and blue a boys' color, reversing earlier norms, and cite a 2017 survey on families encouraging gender-crossing play.

segments.title: Empowering dolls and Earring Magic Ken
segments.summary: The hosts discuss dolls that empower girls, including Barbie's many careers and an American Girl character with lesbian aunts. They describe the 1993 Earring Magic Ken doll and its popularity in the gay community.

segments.title: Etymology of doll and ancient dolls
segments.summary: The word doll is linked to Dorothy as a nickname, and its earliest use in the 1500s was as a pet name for a girlfriend or spouse. It became a child's toy term around 1700. Ancient Egyptian paddle dolls, possibly ritual percussion instruments, and Ghanaian Akua'ba ritual dolls are discussed.

segments.title: Roman and Greek dolls
segments.summary: Roman dolls modeled grown women as idealized wives and mothers. Greek girls dedicated dolls to Artemis when marrying, and unmarried girls were buried with theirs.

segments.title: Rag dolls and Bangwell Putt
segments.summary: Rag dolls are fabric and perishable, so few ancient examples survive; the oldest known is a roughly 2000-year-old linen doll from Egypt. The oldest rag doll in North America, Bangwell Putt, belonged to blind girl Clarissa Field, born 1765, and is kept in Deerfield, Massachusetts. The faceless design may relate to corn husk doll legends.
topics: oldest rag doll in North America

segments.title: Faceless dolls joke
segments.summary: A light exchange about what features a faceless doll lacks, with the hosts joking about facial features.

segments.title: Victorian dolls, porcelain, and death kits
segments.summary: Doll making became an art in 15th-century Germany for aristocratic families. Victorian dolls were made of porcelain, dressed fashionably, and served as status symbols. After Prince Albert's death in 1861, mourning culture reached dolls, and girls received death kits. Victorian dollhouses reflected aristocratic ideals of домаш life.

segments.title: Topsy turvy doll and racist dolls of the Jim Crow era
segments.summary: The topsy turvy doll had two heads, one white and one Black, and is thought to have originated in the Antebellum South among enslaved Black women. Jim Crow-era catalog dolls, including those sold by Montgomery Ward, were racist and reinforced racial hierarchy in children.

segments.title: Clark doll tests and Brown v. Board of Education
segments.summary: Mamie and Kenneth Clark's 1940s doll tests showed Black children assigning positive traits to white dolls and negative ones to Black dolls. The research was used in NAACP cases that were part of Brown v. Board of Education, which overturned school segregation.

segments.title: Sarah Lee doll and Baby Nancy
segments.summary: The Sarah Lee doll, made in 1951, was the first realistic Black baby doll produced in the US. Baby Nancy, from the Black-owned company Shindana Toys, followed during the Black Power movement and was the first doll with realistic Afrocentric features and was a hot seller in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next segment.

segments.title: Paper dolls
segments.summary: Paper dolls were a trend from about 1890 to 1920 and remained popular into the 1970s. They came with paper outfits from magazines and newspapers, and companies like Pillsbury used them to sell products. The hosts also mention a modern magnetic fashion kit.

segments.title: Kewpie, Raggedy Ann, and the Conjuring
segments.summary: Kewpie dolls were a major early twentieth-century doll, later overtaken by Mickey Mouse merchandise and Raggedy Ann. Raggedy Ann began as a Johnny Gruelle book for his daughter, and the doll was later featured in movies, TV, and a Broadway musical. The hosts discuss Annabelle from The Conjuring films.

segments.title: Talking dolls: Betsy Wetsy, Magic Potty Baby, Chatty Cathy, Edison
segments.summary: Betsy Wetsy, made by Ideal in 1937, could drink, wet, and cry. Magic Potty Baby in the early 1990s came with a toilet. Chatty Cathy, a Mattel doll that followed Barbie, had a pull string with phrases. Thomas Edison tried a talking doll in 1890, and a clip of its recitation was played. The Twilight Zone episode Living Doll was inspired by Chatty Cathy. Voice actors for Chatty Cathy included June Foray, Cindy Lee, and Maureen McCormick.

segments.title: Polly Pocket
segments.summary: Polly Pocket began when Chris Wiggs built a miniature dollhouse for his daughter from a makeup compact in the early 1980s. Mattel licensed it as a doll in the early 1990s. A movie adaptation is in development starring Lily Collins, with Reese Witherspoon's company involved.

segments.title: American Girl dolls
segments.summary: Pleasant Rowland, an elementary school teacher in Wisconsin, created American Girl dolls to teach history, starting in 1986 through mail order. They later sold in their own stores.

segments.title: Reborn and realistic baby dolls and dementia care
segments.summary: Realistic reborn baby dolls, sold by FAO Schwarz and companies like Ashton Drake, are handmade collectibles that look and feel like infants. Collectors and some people with dementia or Alzheimer's use them, with benefits and critics noted about dignity.

segments.title: Hasbro's boys' doll Buddy L and Chucky
segments.summary: In 1985, Hasbro launched a doll for boys during the Cabbage Patch craze, described by a marketing executive as soft macho. The hosts link the doll to the Chucky character in Child's Play, which Hasbro never confirmed.

segments.title: Pediophobia and creepy dolls
segments.summary: Pediophobia is the fear of dolls, which can cause panic attacks and may stem from a traumatic experience. Little Miss No Name, released in 1965 with Margaret Keane-style big eyes, is considered creepy. The hosts note that children often don't find dolls creepy, citing the Creepy Chloe account, and mention the Uncanny Valley episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the Christmas episode, wish listeners happy holidays, and invite mail to the show email address.
